papers.title: Frontier models need only one text to unmask its human or AI author
papers.summary: This study shows that state‑of‑the‑art language models can determine whether a text was written by a human or AI, and can often identify the specific author or the AI lab that produced it, using only a single text and a zero‑shot prompt. The authors evaluate models such as Claude Fable 5.2, GPT‑6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon, and Opus 5.5, finding that Opus correctly names the lab behind 98 % of AI‑generated texts, Fable names the author of 39 % of public peer reviews (78 % in a Nature subset), and identifies 69 % of active Reddit users’ usernames. The paper notes that accuracy depends on the model’s exposure to an author’s prior writing and that simply querying the model about its familiarity with a person predicts its identification success, highlighting a significant threat to online anonymity with limited defenses.

papers.title: Beam Model Technical Report
papers.summary: Beam is a sparse Mixture‑of‑Experts language model with 501.3 B total parameters and 23.4 B active parameters, built for coding, reasoning, and agentic tasks. It is pretrained on 23.8 T tokens, achieves a 1‑million‑token context window through a two‑stage mid‑training phase, and is further fine‑tuned with a large‑scale asynchronous reinforcement‑learning campaign on 10.5 K GB300 GPUs that produced over 100 M rollouts in four weeks. The resulting model delivers frontier‑level reasoning while using 3–4× less inference compute than comparable models, and it refuses or pivots on 88.9 % of harmful requests while complying with 81.5 % of harmless requests, the highest refusal/pivot rate among open‑weight models on the Pareto frontier.

papers.title: GLiDE: A Fast, Calibrated Decision Model Distilled from Reasoning Teachers
papers.summary: The paper introduces GLiDE, a family of fast, confidence‑aware decision models that score candidate answers in a single forward pass. By removing causal masking from full‑attention layers and distilling reasoning knowledge from multiple teachers, GLiDE transfers reasoning benefits to single‑pass inference, and further uses parameter‑free recurrent depth to increase computation without token generation. Across five sizes, GLiDE lies on the performance–parameter Pareto frontier, with the 27B variant achieving a hidden‑set score of 73.37, an expected calibration error of 2.1 % and a median latency of 92.9 ms on a single GPU.

papers.title: Language-Oriented Semantic Modeling for Target Language Extraction
papers.summary: The paper introduces a language‑oriented semantic modeling framework for Target Language Extraction that adds language‑specific semantic representations to the usual acoustic extraction. It adapts a pre‑trained speech semantic model with language‑aware prompt conditioning and parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning to generate target‑language‑focused semantic representations from multilingual mixtures, and then integrates these representations into the extraction model to give structured semantic guidance beyond simple language identity labels. Experiments on the CommonVoiceMix dataset show that this approach consistently improves over acoustic‑only baselines, achieving up to 1.16 dB SI‑SDR gain.

papers.title: Language models represent more about emphasis than they can tell you
papers.summary: The paper investigates how well language models can predict prosodic prominence from text alone, whether they can report it when prompted, and how much the speech signal contributes. They compare frozen and fine‑tuned text models, prompted large language models, and speech models on read English speech labelled for word‑level prominence, finding that all text models achieve at most 68.8 % accuracy on a 3‑way task and make similar errors, while prompting LLMs does not improve performance beyond a word‑majority baseline even with 500 examples; linear probes reveal more information in the models’ representations, and speech models reach 84.7 % accuracy. The authors conclude that text alone only captures part of prominence, and that the remaining emphasis must be heard, with LLMs encoding where emphasis falls but not conveying it when asked.
